The shutdown hits all users at once. That is why it is the kind of case in which bodies such as Procon, which is the state consumer protection agency, as well as the Public Defender's Office and the Public Prosecutor's Office can act, and the channels page presents each one.

The sixth mechanism is coordinated institutional action. Without opening a parallel regulatory front, the subsection shows that open auditability and functional equivalence can also guide the action of protection bodies in platform markets.<1>p. 662</1>
How far does this protection go when the service ends?

The company is not obliged to keep the service running forever, and the right to close or reorganize the business still exists. What can be asked depends on what is technically and legally possible, and you do not become the owner of the game, the work or the code.
When the service ends because the company went bankrupt, the question of what happens to what was inside it still has no ready answer. For now it remains open.
Nor is it necessary to resort to a strong idea of consumer ownership over the digital good in order to demand minimum stability.<1>p. 708</1>

The online store hides who paid for placement and who is trustworthy. Does that count? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The online store hides who paid for placement and who is trustworthy.</1> <2>Does that count?</2>

In an online store with many sellers, the so-called marketplace, you choose among what the platform put up front, with the badges, ratings and highlights it organizes. That counts, because the order of the storefront, the label on paid ads and the reputation displayed are part of what the platform supplies.
Consumers do not choose in a vacuum, before a transparent and symmetrical universe of offers. They choose within a field the platform has already pre-interpreted.<1>p. 762</1>
How do you know whether the storefront weighed on your choice?

The store does not just bring buyers and sellers together. It chooses what shows up first, what stays hidden, who looks trustworthy and what can be compared. Without that storefront, the product would not even have reached you the way it did.

What matters is how prominently a product is featured, how trustworthy a seller appears, how reviews are shown and whether an ad was paid for or appeared without payment. The payment method, the delivery, how categories are organized and how alternatives are displayed matter too.

When the same company organizes the storefront and also profits from what happens in it, the situation becomes more serious. The storefront can bring certain offers closer, make others disappear and make a paid ad look like an ordinary result. That is why many options on the screen do not, by themselves, guarantee a real choice.

What is offered, in legally relevant terms, is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics without which the final object does not become economically legible, socially rankable or practically accessible in the terms in which the platform itself presents it.<1>p. 761</1>

The prominent position of an item, the appearance of reliability of a seller, the way reviews are displayed, the distinction between sponsored and organically prioritized products, integration with payment and logistics, the organization of categories and the way alternatives are displayed are all elements that materially interfere with the consumption experience.<1>p. 762</1>

Homogenization does not occur only at the level of the product or the contract. It can be produced by the governance of the interface itself, when the environment artificially brings certain offers closer, renders others invisible, shifts what is sponsored into the zone of the apparently organic, manipulates comparability and manages the user's perception of what is worth more, appears more or seems more trustworthy. The illusion of plurality may thus coexist with severe compression of the real conditions of choice.<1>p. 770</1>
Which storefront screens are worth saving?

The product that arrived shows only the end of the story. The search page is worth saving too, with the order of the offers, the sponsored label or its absence, the reviews, the seller's badge and the delivery promise.

Dated screenshots and screen recordings help show how the storefront looked at the time of purchase. The ranking, the highlight, the seller's rating and the sponsorship show a market that reached you already selected.

It is not enough to examine the final product acquired or the individual content removed, prioritized or hidden. It is necessary to reconstruct the architecture of the experience. This includes, depending on the case, the way offers are presented, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of reviews and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the signals of reliability provided by the interface, the context in which content appears, the relevant moderation criteria and the mechanisms by which the platform induces a perception of market, consensus or priority.<1>p. 763</1>

The first source of support is interface and decision-flow trails: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, remaining time, discount, event or change.<1>p. 607</1>
In marketplaces, it may involve the way ranking, prominence, seller rating and sponsorship logic produce a perceptible market that has already been preselected.<1>p. 763</1>
What can you demand from whoever builds the storefront?

The conversation can go beyond the product and reach the way the storefront is built. It is fair to ask whether it was clear who was selling and what role the platform played, whether paid ads could be told apart from the rest and whether the reputation on display could be checked. It is also fair to ask whether unclear criteria made comparison harder or whether the screen misled you.

The request may include minimum clarity about the criteria that determine order, prominence and reputation, without the company having to open up its internal systems. When it changes the rules and that significantly downgrades what the store offered, restoring what was lost may be in order.

It becomes necessary to examine, through the lens of the IOC, whether there was adequate information about the nature of the intermediation, whether the distinction between organic priority and sponsored priority was materially intelligible, whether the reputation displayed was functionally verifiable, whether the opacity of the criteria compromised relevant comparability and whether the interface itself produced deceptiveness, obscuring or structural asymmetry incompatible with the consumer regime.<1>p. 764</1>

Open auditability requires minimum institutional verifiability of the relevant criteria of presentation, prioritization, moderation, reputation and circulation, without this implying unrestricted opening of internal systems.<1>p. 764</1>

Functional equivalence, in turn, applies when changes to the intermediation regime, the visibility logic, the reputational criteria or the circulation rules significantly degrade the utility legitimately incorporated into the relationship, without compatible restoration.<1>p. 764</1>
Where can you take a complaint about how the store displays its offers?

The first step is usually the store itself, in writing and with the screens saved. The complaint does not have to stop at the purchase that went wrong, because the way the storefront highlighted and hid the offers also counts. That holds even when none of it was written in the contract or the ad.

When the same unclear criterion for ordering or reputation affects everyone who buys there, the response can be collective. Procon, Consumidor.gov.br and the Public Prosecutor's Office are options described on the channels page.

This subtype has recurring blind spots that must be avoided. The first is the tendency to treat the interface as mere visual support, and not as a constitutive part of the supply. The second is the tendency to imagine that the platform would be legally liable only for what it stated expressly in a clause or in advertising, as if the effective governance of visibility were legally irrelevant. The third is the tendency to reduce the dispute to the terminal act, such as the failed purchase, the removal of a piece of content or the supposed preference for a given offer, without investigating the private structure of salience that conditioned the user's entire experience.<1>p. 763</1>

An opaque sanctions policy, a non-auditable regime of functional change, an interface logic that dilutes the essential under informational excess, a materially decisive ranking system without usable history or a trust architecture that absorbs and neutralizes contestation before it becomes litigation are all examples of problems whose unity lies in the design, not in the episode.<1>p. 775</1>
When is the storefront's ordering no reason to complain?

Not every way of organizing the storefront is illegal, and not every intermediation problem is solved by consumer law. The question is whether the lack of clarity hindered your choice in a relevant way.

Also left out, in principle, is the store that only sells advertising space and customer acquisition, without really controlling the sales that come afterward. Buying online does not, by itself, turn any product into a digital object governed by the platform.

When the problem is only a defect in the product, an improper charge or a delivery that never happened, ordinary consumer law tends to solve it. In that case the storefront does not need to enter the conversation.

The second limit is the scenario in which the platform functions as a channel or storefront, but does not govern, in structural terms, the acquired utility, lacking the infrastructural centrality characteristic of the IOC. This is the case that rules out, in principle, the marketplace that provides positioning and customer acquisition services through advertising, but does not exercise relevant material interference over the effective governance of subsequent commercial operations.<1>p. 434</1>

Curation, ranking, reputation, dispute policies, display criteria, delivery parameters and verification mechanisms structure the possibility of finding, comparing, contracting and validating what is acquired. This is not to say that every digital mediation automatically converts any good into an IOC.<1>p. 487</1>

The service's currency now buys less. Is that allowed? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The service's currency now buys less.</1> <2>Is that allowed?</2>

You bought in-app currency with real money, like a game's coins or an app's credits, and now the same item costs more coins. The company that sells the currency is the same one that sets the prices inside, and that is why the change needs to be looked at carefully.

Riot does not describe the game's currency as a simple neutral medium of exchange. It treats it as part of a closed circuit, whose equivalence can be recalibrated unilaterally. The terms admit that, “sometimes”, the company may change the purchasing power of the In-Game Currency, including by increasing the number of coins needed to acquire virtual products such as skins, and place this movement under the generic promise of notice and gradualness <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 176</3>

What is observed, however, in platform-governed immaterial consumption, is an inversion of logic. The supplier does not limit itself to competing within a market. It designs the very world of reference in which consumption takes place, controls catalog, visibility, rules of circulation, the practical unit of account and conditions of permanence, and then begins to exercise, simultaneously, functions analogous to those of a market and of a normative authority, defining on its own the level of prices and the pace of internal inflation.<1>p. 179</1>
How do you know whether the change in the currency affected what you had?
The loss can come in several ways. The item starts costing more coins, prices change by region and bonuses on currency purchases come and go. And certain event currencies simply expire after a date.

When prices are given in in-app currency, in bundles and in conversions, it becomes hard to know how much you are really spending and to compare it with anything else. Each currency works like a language of its own, and you are the one who has to translate everything.

A change in what the currency buys goes through the same test as other changes. The question is not whether the company keeps selling something under the same name. It is whether what you acquired remains equivalent to what justified your trust and your spending.

Likewise, the instability of the real cost is not limited to the internal design of the store. It also appears when the platform adjusts economic parameters by region and runs bonuses that reconfigure, by time window, the perceived advantage of buying paid currency.<1>p. 398</1>

Thus, by adopting as a procedure the creation of multiple currencies that do not merge and have multiple durations within the ecosystem, including expiring entirely when their scheduled period ends, the platform stands out for further aggravating the user's difficulty in understanding the real value of what the user is able to acquire, giving rise to and mobilizing, above all, the fear of missing out in its users.<1>p. 398</1>

The consumer no longer deals with a price that can be compared and audited in a straight line, and begins to deal with multiple internal grammars that require situational reading, because each currency “speaks” a different language.<1>p. 397</1>

The strength of the criterion appears clearly in scenarios such as removals of relevant functionalities, nerfs that hollow out acquired utility, interface changes that disrupt ordinary use, redefinitions of rules that lower the equivalence of what was promised, changes in currency or internal purchasing power, mutations in progression systems, reclassifications of rarity, deletion or compression of inventories, and changes in visibility patterns that affect the consumer's position in the ecosystem. In all these cases, the decisive question should not be whether the platform kept offering “something” under the same label. The correct question is whether the thing legally acquired, as a position of enjoyment in a governed environment, retains sufficient functional equivalence with what was the object of the consumer's expectation, trust and investment.<1>p. 637-638</1>
Which records show how much your currency was worth?

It is worth keeping how much you paid in reais for each bundle, the balance you had and the coin price of the items that matter, before and after the change. The company's notice also deserves to be kept, because the contract of a major game promises to give notice when a change affects the currency in a negative and significant way.
For currencies that expire, it helps to write down the expiration dates that appeared on the screen, because the deadline is part of the system's own rule.

We normally do this only in progressive steps, but you will be notified (through posts on our website, app or game) if we intend to make changes that significantly affect your In-Game Currency in a negative way.<1>p. 614</1>
This shows that urgency does not depend on an external emotional appeal, because expiration is designed as a rule of the token system itself.<1>p. 398</1>
What can you ask for when the currency is worth less?

The request may include clear information about how much each item costs and about what changed. The ad, the value and the costs that did not show need to match what you receive. Depending on the case, the lack of clarity may also lead to restoring what you lost because of it.

If the change means that what you already had is no longer worth the same, it is fair to ask that the loss be restored, corrected or reviewed. And the same contract says that price adjustments apply to the future, except for what you have already acquired. That may help you demand that what you already bought be left untouched.

We may adjust the prices of any part of the Riot Services at any time (with future effect, that is, with the exception of what you have already acquired). This may affect the purchasing power of your In-Game Currency, although we normally do so only in gradual steps.<1>p. 614</1>
Who can you turn to when a change to the currency affects everyone?

The first step is usually the company itself. The contract that says the currency is non-refundable makes an exception for when your consumer rights guarantee a refund. That is why the answer does not stop at what is written there.

A change in the currency affects everyone who has a balance at the same time. That is why it is the kind of case that can go to Procon, the Public Defender's Office or the Public Prosecutor's Office, which the channels page describes. In these cases the response can target the whole rule, and not just your balance.
Is changing the price of the currency always forbidden?

No. A company can, often legitimately, set its own prices, especially when there is real competition and you can switch services without losing everything. The problem appears when leaving is costly, comparison becomes hard and the value depends only on what the company decides.
Nor is the service's economy required to stand still. Rebalancing and adjustments can happen, and what is not allowed is using the change to destroy the value of what you already had.

It is important to note that functional value equivalence does not freeze the ecosystem. It does not require absolute identity between before and after, nor does it prohibit rebalancing, adjustments, corrections or developments of the environment. What it prevents is the use of mutability as a screen for the opportunistic destruction of value.<1>p. 638</1>

It happened to a lot of people. Can it be solved all at once? · Lex Plataformae
<1>It happened to a lot of people.</1> <2>Can it be solved all at once?</2>

The same problem hit a lot of people in the same service, and each person was left alone with it, thinking it was bad luck. When the loss arises from the very design of the service, the response can be collective and change how it works for everyone, but it is not enough that many people complain about the same thing.

In platform environments, the harmful source may lie in the very design of the supply regime, so that the unity of the problem does not stem primarily from the empirical repetition of episodes, but from the permanence of a single, repeatable and functionally expansive structure producing loss, opacity and asymmetry. The injury, then, is not only plural. It is architectural.<1>p. 774</1>
How do you know whether the problem lies in the design rather than in each case?
The sign is a single origin that recurs and is part of the normal way the service works. The cases do not need to be identical, because what repeats is the source of the problem.

The ranking is the order in which the platform shows offers or people. Some examples are an unclear punishment policy, changes that leave no trace and a ranking that decides everything without any usable history. Also included are the screen that hides the essential amid too much information and the customer service that absorbs the complaint before it becomes a dispute.

The effects are not the same for everyone, but the origin is common. That is why the difficulty of proving it, when everyone runs into it, may be part of the way the service works and not your own failure.
The typology reveals precisely that certain harms are programmatic. Not because all cases are the same, but because the source of their production remains structurally the same.<1>p. 776</1>

A merely atomized treatment of the conflict tends to produce two bad results. On the one hand, it monetizes episodes without altering the machine that reproduces them. On the other, it turns the systemic difficulty of proof into the private failure of dispersed consumers, each obliged to face alone an informational regime designed precisely to hinder reconstruction.<1>p. 776</1>
What can each person keep to help show the pattern?

Your case still matters, and it is worth keeping the dated screens, the company's notices and the messages exchanged with it. It also helps to show that the same thing repeats and how the pieces of the service combine to produce the loss.
Reports from other users are not the main proof of a problem. Even so, they can help show a long experience that keeps recurring and a policy that affects many people.

Community reports are not the central proof of an unlawful act, but they are useful to formulate and illustrate a long-lasting, even if hypothetical, consumer experience in which one glimpses the restriction and sedimentation of a broad punitive policy over the Brazilian base<1>p. 611</1>
What can a collective response ask for that a single case cannot?

The collective response can ask for measures that stop the loss from continuing and that make the service checkable from then on. These include keeping minimum records, giving a checkable reason for relevant punishments, maintaining an accessible history of changes and explaining the minimum criteria for distribution, priority and ranking.

Collective redress thus proves particularly suited to imposing injunctive, procedural and analytical measures capable of reintroducing institutional verifiability into the environment. This may involve duties to preserve minimum records, a requirement of verifiable reasons for materially relevant sanctions, maintenance of an accessible history of relevant changes, explanation of minimum operational criteria of distribution, priority or ranking, and other measures that are aimed not only at repairing past harms, but at reorganizing the future conditions of controllability of enjoyment.<1>p. 775</1>
Who can take everyone's problem forward?

Those who act on behalf of everyone are the collective standing parties and the public protection and oversight bodies. The collective standing parties are the institutions the law authorizes to defend an entire group. Among them are the Public Prosecutor's Office, the Public Defender's Office and consumer protection bodies, such as Procon. When the problem lies precisely in the lack of records and clarity, that lack can become the very object of the collective request. That way the debate moves from isolated episodes to the way the service is built.

It is at this point that open auditability turns from a dogmatic standard into a condition for the effectiveness of collective redress. Without it, the action of collective standing parties, administrative protection bodies and regulatory and oversight structures tends to run into the same opacity that already hinders individual reaction. With it, it becomes possible to turn the requirement of verifiability into the main object of protection, shifting the debate from isolated episodes to the shaping of the environment.<1>p. 776</1>
When is a large number of affected people not enough for a collective response?
It is not enough that many people complain about similar facts, because the number alone does not yet show a common origin in the design of the service.
The collective response also does not replace the claim of someone who lost something concrete. It targets the source of the problem, while the individual claim is still needed to repair your loss.

The basis of collective redress, here, does not lie only in the circumstance that many consumers may be affected by similar facts. That finding, though relevant, would still remain too dependent on a quantitative logic.<1>p. 774</1>

Collective redress, on the contrary, allows the manifestations to be traced back to their unitary source. This does not mean abolishing the role of individual protection. It remains indispensable, above all for the repair of concretely experienced losses and for the situated reconstruction of certain specific impacts.<1>p. 775</1>

An item I received as a gift was removed from my account. Now what? · Lex Plataformae
<1>An item I received as a gift was removed from my account.</1> <2>Now what?</2>

You received an item as a gift through the game's official feature, and later it disappeared from your account because there was fraud somewhere along the way. When the fraud passes through a feature the company itself offers, the risk is part of its business and cannot fall entirely on whoever received it in good faith.
How do you know whether your gift fits this situation?

The situation is that of someone who received a gift through an official channel, or bought game currency on a site that looked legitimate, and later lost items or had the account suspended. Sometimes the whole account goes back to an earlier state, which is called a rollback, and takes along items you had obtained through normal means.

What usually lies behind it is the chargeback, which happens when someone disputes the card purchase and the bank reverses the payment. The company's rule for these cases may punish not only whoever sent the gift, but also whoever received it.

It matters a lot whether the feature was official. In one concrete case, sending gifts was a regular feature, inside the game and with rules and limits, so the trust of those who received gifts was created by the company itself.

At the same time, outside stores sold the game currency as something safe and advantageous, and no one made clear what was official, tolerated or forbidden. That is why one cannot presume that anyone would know how to tell legitimate resale apart from cloned-card fraud.

The company deactivated the gifting feature on the Brazilian server for a long period, suppressed received assets and carried out regressive restorations or blocks on affected accounts, without any equivalent effort being seen, within its private policy, of consistent individualization between intentional fraud, excusable error, acquisition through an apparently reliable channel and the recipient's good faith.<1>p. 611</1>

There is a recent report of a rollback with the permanent disappearance of skins and other cosmetics that the consumer claims to have acquired legitimately through different ordinary means, in a context in which reconstructing the origin of each item becomes extremely burdensome and fragmented.<1>p. 616</1>

The gifting feature did not operate on the margins of the platform, nor did it constitute a clandestine or intrinsically deviant practice. On the contrary, Riot itself presented it as a regular feature, integrated into the game client, subject to objective eligibility requirements, quantitative limits, regional restrictions and standardized sending flows.<1>p. 610</1>

Gifting was part of the ordinary architecture of the service. The consumer's trust in the lawfulness of the circulation of virtual content through this channel was not a subjective whim. It was trust produced by the platform itself and supported by an officially offered feature<1>p. 610</1>

The market for Riot Points and external codes was crossed by a semiotic gray zone, in which promotional materials and digital storefronts presented the external purchase of virtual currency as an ordinary, safe, advantageous practice compatible with the game's ecosystem. The language used in these environments mimicked commercial legitimacy, visual professionalism, subsequent functional integration with the official client, plausible promises of savings and a rhetoric of security. In this setting, it is not legally serious to presume that the average consumer would always distinguish, with sufficient clarity, a tolerated partner, legitimate resale, a gray market and fraud linked to a cloned card. The vulnerability does not stem from private naivety, but from the absence of robust communicational demarcation between what was admitted, tolerated, official or forbidden.<1>p. 611-612</1>
What helps prove where each item came from?

After the items disappear, you are left with the task of reconstructing, one by one, where each item came from. That is why the purchase emails, the card statements and the old screenshots of the inventory and of the gifts received are worth so much.

If the currency was bought on an outside site, it helps to keep how that site presented itself, with the ad, the promise of security and the professional look, because that shows why the purchase seemed legitimate.
The rest stays with the company, such as the transaction history, the origin of the removed items and the criterion used to return the account to an earlier state.

The episode shows how the platform, by carrying out a broad reversal of the account's state, transfers to the player the almost archaeological burden of reconstructing item by item what was already part of his sphere of enjoyment.<1>p. 616</1>

The language used in these environments mimicked commercial legitimacy, visual professionalism, subsequent functional integration with the official client, plausible promises of savings and a rhetoric of security.<1>p. 612</1>

The fifth is that of evidentiary asymmetry, with the need to preserve trails, transaction histories, the origin of the removed items, the criteria used for the rollback and individualized justification of the measures adopted.<1>p. 617</1>
What can you ask to get back?

When no individual and consistent proof rules out your good faith, you may ask for the removed items to come back and for your account to be restored. You can also ask the company to keep and show the records and to explain why the measure affected you in particular.
The request may also include that the company state clearly where it is safe to buy and that it stop applying rules that place the whole risk of fraud on the buyer.

The terms of use, which are the contract accepted when creating the account, call what you have a revocable license, a permission to use that the company says it can withdraw. That label is not enough to put the system's failure on you. The company itself showed there was another way when, in another of its games, it began to prefer payment methods less exposed to disputes.

Here, the consumer regime accommodates requests for functional restoration of the position of enjoyment, restoration of assets when the user's good faith has not been refuted by robust individualized proof, preservation and disclosure of minimum records of the supply, informational correction about legitimate acquisition channels and neutralization of clauses or practices that transfer entirely to the consumer the structural risks of the system.<1>p. 617</1>

In another title of the same ecosystem, the company began to favor payment instruments less exposed to later disputes, such as prepaid cards and single-use codes, with strong discouragement of purchases on unauthorized third-party sites. The move is telling: the response to the chargeback risk was not only punitive, but also reorganized the transactional environment toward means more controllable from the supplier's point of view. This confirms that there were structural alternatives for mitigating the risk.<1>p. 616-617</1>
Who should you take the case to when many people lost gifts at the same time?

The first request goes to the company itself, with what you kept about the origin of the items. If the answer is only that the terms of use allow the content to be removed, the case can go on through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, paths that the channels page details.
In a lawsuit, you can ask the company to show the records that only it has. If it does not cooperate, certain facts may start to count in your favor.
When the measure affects many players at once, the case also lends itself to a collective response, which can correct the rule for everyone.

Instead of treating fraud as a structural problem of its own transactional environment, Riot redistributed the risk to an undifferentiated mass of consumers, suppressed assets, interrupted an official content-circulation feature and imposed sanctions based on broad presumptions of co-responsibility, including on users who did not knowingly take part in the fraud.<1>p. 610</1>
Is every purchase made outside the game protected?

Buying outside the game does not bring automatic protection. What matters is whether the channel seemed legitimate and whether you acted in good faith, because the difference between deliberate fraud and a gift received in good faith still holds.
Getting items back depends on your good faith not having been ruled out by individual and consistent proof.
Reports from other players help show the picture, but on their own they do not prove what happened. And asking is not the same as getting, because each case depends on what can be shown.

Here, the consumer regime accommodates requests for functional restoration of the position of enjoyment, restoration of assets when the user's good faith has not been refuted by robust individualized proof<1>p. 617</1>

The offer said last chance. Was I pressured into buying? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The offer said last chance.</1> <2>Was I pressured into buying?</2>

The countdown, the limited edition or the notice that the item would disappear made you decide quickly, perhaps before you understood everything you were buying. The store itself may have set up that rush, and what matters is when it comes with hidden information and no real chance to compare.

The first family of these techniques is that of artificial scarcity and manufactured urgency. Its mechanism is well known. Short windows, accelerated rotation of offers, countdown timers, “limited editions”, ephemeral events and temporary benefits are used to shift the decision from the field of rational comparison to that of reactive response.<1>p. 670</1>
How do you know whether the rush was manufactured?

A digital item could be sold to everyone, at any time, without running out. When it only appears in short windows, disappears, comes back now and then or becomes a last chance, that scarcity is the seller's choice, not the nature of the item.

The rush can also come in series, with passes, time-bound goals, staged events and rewards that depend on always coming back. In this arrangement, giving up no longer just means stopping and comes to mean losing what you accumulated and falling behind the others.

The strongest sign is the combination. The urgency is highlighted, while the limits of use, the chance that the item will change and the possible losses stay in a corner. And you do not need to prove that someone meant to rush you.

In digital objects, the marginal cost of reproduction tends to fall drastically and, in theory, availability could expand without requiring productive capacity comparable to the factory, logistics and the extraction of inputs. Therefore, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, one is not facing a natural condition of the object, but a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as a fact, but as a project<1>p. 209</1>

Teasers, pre-sales, conditioned progressions, passes, serialized rewards and temporary goals build a trajectory in which value no longer resides only in the object and comes to reside in the cost of “falling behind”. The relevant legal effect is the conversion of enjoyment into a directed path, in which giving up no longer means a mere interruption of consumption and comes to represent loss of accumulated value, regression of position and discontinuity of an expectation already installed.<1>p. 670-671</1>

The supplier emphasizes urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige, but relegates to side conditions what really defines the substance of enjoyment, such as relevant limitations of use, the ordinary mutability of the object, equivalence parameters, possible losses, restricted windows of use, additional requirements for fulfilling the promise or specific conditions for maintaining the advertised value.<1>p. 631</1>
Which screens show the rush after the offer is over?

It is worth keeping the screen with the remaining time, the limited edition notice and the offer as it appeared, with a date. It also helps to note when the same campaign or the same last chance came back, because the repetition shows that the urgency was the store's routine.

For passes and events, the event rules, the time-bound goals, the announcements of what was coming and the changes made midway are useful. With them you can compare the promise at the start with what was delivered at the end.

The minimum sign of proof, here, does not depend on intuition about manipulation. It appears in remaining-time screens, in the history of repeated temporary campaigns, in the programmed rotation of offers and in the very visual architecture that brings the benefit forward and postpones the relevant condition.<1>p. 670</1>
What can you ask for when you were rushed into the purchase?

The request can start with information. When the store uses intensity and scarcity to rush the decision, it needs to show the essentials right there, at the time of purchase, prominently, in a way that allows comparison and at the right moment.
If what was sold as a one-time chance did not deliver what it promised, you may also ask for the offer to be fulfilled or corrected and for you to recover what you lost.

When the rush combines with staged rarity, lack of clarity and difficulty in backing out, and this repeats as a pattern, consumer law may treat the whole as an abusive practice. Then the request can go beyond your purchase and reach the very design of the store.

When artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency, cycles of promise, manufacture of risk, asymmetric frictions and hindered reversibility operate in a predictable and repeated way to exploit semiotic vulnerability and govern the consumer's choice, the problem no longer lies only in the final quality of the performance, but in the very way the supplier organizes the relationship.<1>p. 676</1>
Who can you turn to when the last chance comes back every week?
The company itself is the first place to go, with the screens you saved, to ask for the missing information or for the offer to be corrected.

If the company does not resolve it, the case can go on through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, paths that the channels page details. Since manufactured urgency is usually the store's routine, and not something that happened only to you, it lends itself to a collective response, through a class action or through public consumer protection bodies.
Is every limited-time promotion illegal?
No. A time-limited promotion, a limited edition and a reward are not illegal just for existing, nor when they appear on their own.

The problem may lie in the sum of pieces that, one by one, look harmless. The rush starts to matter when it works together with a lack of clarity, in a stable and repeated way, against good faith, which is the duty of loyalty between the parties.

In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, unlawfulness may lie precisely in the articulation between elements that, seen separately, seem neutral, but that, combined, govern the consumer's decision in a structurally asymmetric way.<1>p. 632</1>

Scarcity, urgency, serialized promise, threat of loss, functional erosion and symbolic dependence are not unlawful for existing in the abstract nor for appearing in isolation. They become teleologically abusive when they operate in combination with opacity and permanent asymmetry, in a stable and replicable pattern, directing enjoyment toward ends incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability of the supply.<1>p. 674</1>

The service requires a program that runs on my device. Can I question it? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The service requires a program that runs on my device.</1> <2>Can I question it?</2>

Some services only work if you install a program that runs in the background of your computer and starts up with it, even with the game closed. Fighting cheating is legitimate, but the word security does not end the discussion about how far the company can control your machine.

The platform's private sovereignty, in other words, no longer governs only the game and begins to contest the minimum conditions of reliability of the user's own machine. Under the vocabulary of security, this expansion usually appears as if it were mere technical inevitability. But the discourse of security does not, by itself, neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture adopted.<1>p. 522</1>
How do you know whether the program goes beyond what the service needs?

The clearest example is that of an anti-cheat program that runs in the kernel, which is the deepest layer of the operating system, the one that controls how the machine works. It starts when the computer starts, and the company can block the game if it is turned off or removed.

The terms of use, which are the contract you accept when creating the account, also allow the company to monitor, inside your device, the use of the service and to require new programs and updates. And they leave the cost of adapting the equipment to you.

Also included here are requests to change the machine's startup settings and the blocking of other legitimate programs. The company itself acknowledges that changing these settings the wrong way can cause serious problems on the computer.
Fighting cheating is a legitimate interest. The question is whether that interest is enough for the company to gain so much power over your equipment without stronger control.

Riot's Terms of Service not only allow active monitoring on the user's device and the running of anti-cheat software in the background, but also reserve to the company the power to change, update, restrict features, require software and compulsory updates, redistribute to the user the costs of technical adaptation and limit its own financial exposure.<1>p. 526</1>

The serious legal question was never whether there is a legitimate interest in preserving competitive integrity; of course there is. The question is another: whether that interest is enough to authorize, without reinforced control, the expansion of the supplier's technical power over the material base of the consumer's equipment.<1>p. 532</1>
What should you record about the program and your computer?

It is worth keeping the screens that asked for the installation or the change of settings, the notices about the program and the date each requirement appeared, because some show up after the purchase, with mandatory updates.
If the computer starts crashing, the failure logs that the system itself generates help. In one reported case, it was by reading these logs that the user linked the failures to the program.

In one of the cases, the user reports recurring BSOD and links the problem to the file vgk.sys, that is, to the low-level driver tied to Vanguard, based on reading the system's own minidumps<1>p. 529</1>
What can you demand from the company about this program?

You can ask for clear information about what the program does, what data it processes, for what purpose and who processes that data. The data protection law requires a specific purpose, limitation to what is necessary and transparency, and clicking accept does not settle that on its own.

You can also question whether what is required is really necessary. Consumer law does not allow risks beyond those that are normal and foreseeable, and an architecture that increases the risk to the device falls under that safety control.

In borderline cases, when the program brings risks and the information about them was insufficient, it may even be treated as a defective or poorly informed product, which opens the door to holding the company liable.

The processing of data linked to Vanguard cannot be justified en bloc under the generic heading of “security”, because it must observe a legitimate, specific, explicit and informed purpose, necessity, with limitation to the indispensable minimum, and transparency, with clear, precise and accessible information. It also requires an adequate legal basis, is not automatically satisfied by ritualized and generic acceptances, and presupposes technical and administrative measures capable of effectively protecting the data.<1>p. 533</1>

The CDC does not allow Vanguard to be rendered invisible as if it were a mere engineering option. Products and services placed on the market may not entail risks to health or safety beyond those normal and foreseeable for their nature and enjoyment, and the supplier may not place into circulation a product or service that it knows or should know presents a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness.<1>p. 532-533</1>

If the architecture intensifies systemic risk, enlarges the attack surface, requires deep technical configurations and may radiate instability to the equipment, then it comes onto the radar of consumer safety control.<1>p. 533</1>

In borderline hypotheses, liability itself for design defects or for insufficient or inadequate information on use and risks reopens the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product.<1>p. 533</1>
Who can you ask what the program does on your computer?
The first request for information goes to the company itself, which must state clearly the reach of the program, the risks and who processes your data, without hiding behind the word security.
If it does not answer or if the program causes damage to your equipment, the case can go on through Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, paths that the channels page details.

It also requires an adequate legal basis, is not automatically satisfied by ritualized and generic acceptances, and presupposes technical and administrative measures capable of effectively protecting the data. In other words, the platform cannot invoke security as a totalizing justification while maintaining opacity about the reach, necessity and agents of the processing. Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security.<1>p. 533</1>

There are also sources that systematize the case already through the lens of consumer rights and public perception of risk, associating Vanguard with persistent technical presence, absence of a real alternative of refusal, expanded control over the machine and continuous operation outside the strict moment of play. The point is important because it shows that the dispute is neither only technical nor only cultural. It is already perceived as a consumer rights problem, precisely because the enjoyment of the IOC becomes conditioned on a material subordination of the user's equipment to private criteria of security and compatibility.<1>p. 531</1>
Is every deep anti-cheat program illegal?

Not necessarily. A program of this kind is not illegal just because it runs in the deepest part of the machine, and fighting cheating remains legitimate. What is rejected is treating the word security as an explanation that spares the company from showing why so much access is necessary.

Reports from other users about crashes help show the problem, but they do not prove on their own that the program caused the failure. And the extreme case, that of the computer that stops working, is the limit of the problem, and not necessarily the most common one.
Nor is the company being asked to open the program's code. The question is whether the degree of access required is proportional, necessary, transparent and justifiable.

Even the most extreme reports of possible bricking or severe loss of availability of the equipment have illustrative value for the argument, even though they do not authorize conclusive expert claims. Their value lies in showing how the risk radiated to the hardware is part of the empirical reception of the case and speaks directly to the thesis that the governance of the IOC may go beyond the game environment and reach the very material functionality of the machine. It is the limit form of the problem. Not the only one, nor necessarily the most frequent, but the one that makes it impossible to pretend that we are only talking about “just another game software”.<1>p. 531-532</1>
The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the degree of technical interference required of the consumer.<1>p. 523</1>

What was advertised is not what I received. Now what? · Lex Plataformae
<1>What was advertised is not what I received.</1> <2>Now what?</2>

You bought after seeing previews, countdowns, rarity badges or promises of prominence, and what arrived later does not match what all of that led you to expect. When the ad helped shape what you understood you were buying, it becomes part of the offer, and the difference between what was promised and what was delivered can be claimed.
How do you know whether the ad became part of the purchase?

The offer is what the company commits to deliver when it advertises. It is not always in a single sentence, because previews, storefronts, events, countdowns, hints of rarity and promises of prestige or performance can together form the idea of what you were buying.

The deception also does not need to be an outright lie. The ad may suggest that the item is stable when it can change at any moment, that it is rare when the rarity was programmed or that it is worth as much as another when it is not.

The deciding point is whether the ad really weighed on how you understood the item, on the value you gave it and on the decision to buy. When the promise was of prestige or recognition, the failure may not even appear as a technical defect, but as the loss of the place that was sold as the core of the purchase.
The legally relevant promise is not always concentrated in a single statement.<1>p. 725</1>

In immaterial objects of consumption, inducement into error may result from constructed ambiguity, from strategically distributed relevant omission or from a mismatch between the overall meaning of the promise and the real conditions of enjoyment under managed mutability. Advertising may suggest stability where there is structural precariousness, equivalence where there is relevant asymmetry, rarity where there is programmed artificiality, freedom of use where there is asymmetric reversibility, continuity where there is intense mutability.<1>p. 724-725</1>

Where prior communication significantly shapes the reading of the object, becomes part of the perception of its value and conditions the consumer's adherence, there will be an offer in a materially controllable sense.<1>p. 726</1>

Control must therefore capture the overall regime of signification produced by the supplier. This requirement is particularly important in immaterial objects of consumption whose enjoyment depends on visibility, reputation, collective recognition or insertion into an ecosystem of symbolic value. In them, the mismatch between promise and delivery may not manifest itself as an evident technical defect, but as a relevant frustration of the symbolic or relational position presented as part of the core of the acquisition.<1>p. 726</1>
What evidence of the ad is worth saving before it is taken down?

It pays to keep the ads, the previews, the store screens showing what was featured, and the purchase and confirmation screens, all with dates. It also helps to record what happened next, so you can compare the earlier promise with what you were able to use.

These records carry more weight than your memory, because they show how the sales environment was set up. The conversation stops being about what you understood and becomes about what the screen presented.
What can you demand when the delivery fell short of the ad?

You may ask for the offer to be fulfilled or corrected and for the function or position the ad promised, or something equivalent, to be restored to you. When the same message keeps misleading other people, you can also ask for it to stop.

Depending on the case, consumer law may treat this as an offer that binds whoever made it, or as misleading advertising, meaning advertising that creates an image the delivered product does not live up to. It may also treat it as abusive advertising, meaning advertising that exploits the buyer's weak spots to pressure the decision.

When the company promises rarity, performance or an advantage and later downgrades it by criteria no one can check, your frustration need not be dismissed as mere annoyance. It may be a significant failure in the supply itself.

Misleading advertising, in turn, manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in the actual experience of enjoyment, either because the platform later downgrades the object, or because the initial promise already concealed, through ambiguity or through the architecture of visibility, the real way in which the utility would be delivered.<1>p. 631</1>

Abusive advertising, finally, appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing his space for deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, ritualization of acceptance and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.<1>p. 631</1>
Who should you take the gap between the ad and the delivery to?
Your first stop is usually the company itself, with the ad and the screens in hand, because the duty to make what was promised match what was delivered belongs to it.

If the company does not fix it, the case can go to Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, routes explained on the channels page. When the same ad reaches many people, the response can go beyond your case and change the message itself, through a class action or through the work of public consumer protection agencies.
Does every exaggerated ad entitle you to something?

No. Selling with enthusiasm, drawing attention and stirring the desire to buy are part of commerce. What consumer law does not accept is for this to work by hiding the essentials and capturing the buyer's expectation.

What is examined is what was promised as value and as function, what was hidden as cost, limit or fragility, and whether that matches what you received. A loose, upbeat phrase with no weight in your decision is not enough.

The market may promote, persuade, dramatize and organize interest. What the CDC does not allow is for this organization of interest to operate through functional opacity, capture of expectation and displacement of the essential outside the useful field of understanding.<1>p. 631</1>

The records are with the company. How do I prove what happened? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The records are with the company.</1> <2>How do I prove what happened?</2>

In most disputes with platforms, it is the company, not you, that keeps the records of what happened. That is why the work of proving can be divided according to what each side can access, though you still need to give a coherent account of what you went through.

When the platform manages the experience and simultaneously concentrates the traces needed to prove it, the preservation of these elements ceases to be a peripheral question of cooperation and comes to constitute a condition of institutional controllability. The consequence is the admissibility of a dynamic distribution of the burden of proof whenever the relevant evidence is structurally under the supplier's technical control.<1>p. 735</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to require from the consumer a detailed demonstration of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within his reach. This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, argumentative sequencing or delimitation of the disputed object.<1>p. 736</1>
How do you know the lack of proof is not your fault?

It happens when the punishment was automatic, the change left no public trace, the purchase screen has already changed or the history disappeared from the account. In these cases the lack of proof may be an effect of the way the service is organized, and not a weakness of your claim.

The company knows what it showed you, when it showed it, which version was in force, what transaction happened and what rule it used in a punishment. When all of this stays with it alone, whoever controls the service also comes to control the proof.
In environments of governed enjoyment, verifiability is part of the very duty to shape the relationship legitimately.<1>p. 735</1>
What is within your reach and worth keeping right now?

Even without the company's records, a lot is within your reach. Dated screenshots, screen recordings, the purchase and confirmation screens and the messages about rarity, remaining time, discount or change show how the environment was set up.
It also helps to keep what was promised, such as ads, posts and notices, to compare with what you received later. What counts is not your memory, but the form the screen had when you went through it.

This material does not need to prove everything on its own. It serves to show that your account is plausible and how it fits into the service, and that is what allows you to ask the company for the rest.
How do you ask for the records without making the request too vague?

The request works better when it is precise. Instead of asking for all the system's data, it can target the version history of an item or the screens shown at purchase. It can also target the records of a transaction, the notice of change or the reason for a punishment.

In a lawsuit, the judge can order the company to show documents and records it holds. The judge can also divide the work of proving in another way, when it is very hard for you and much easier for the company.

If the company refuses to show them without justification, the facts the document would prove may be accepted as true. Nor does a reply that the data is internal or no longer exists end the conversation.
The judge may order the party to produce a document or thing in its possession<1>p. 659</1>
Art. 400. In deciding the request, the judge shall admit as true the facts that, by means of the document or thing, the party intended to prove<1>p. 660</1>
Who can help take the proof out of the company's hands?

The company must keep and show the minimum records of what happened, so your first request can go to it, stating exactly what you want to see. When questioned, it is up to the company to show that it informed you and that it acted within what it promised.

The strongest tools, such as an order to produce documents or a different division of the work of proving, only work inside a lawsuit. So when all the proof is with the company, it helps to have a lawyer or the Public Defender's Office on your side. The Small Claims Court and the other routes are on the channels page.
Public consumer protection agencies can also use these criteria to require the company, once and for all users, to keep records and offer an understandable way to contest decisions.

The supplier does not fulfill its role merely by throwing information into the environment; it must also demonstrate, when questioned, that it informed adequately, that it regularly exercised its power of change and that the impact produced was compatible with the promised performance.<1>p. 660</1>

In the same sense, the regime for the production of documents or things provided for in arts. 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>1</2></1> offers the most direct route to operationalize open auditability.<3>p. 659</3>
What remains your task?

None of this spares you from telling a coherent, plausible story and making clear what you are disputing. What goes away is the idea that you and the company are on an equal footing when it comes to proof.
A different division of proof is not automatic. It responds to the concrete case and becomes stronger the more the records are concentrated with the company.
Nor does anyone ask for the system's entire code or the company's secrets. The technical examination, called an expert examination, looks only at what changed and the effect it had on what you use.
The more intense the private concentration of records, the greater the requirement of preservation, delimited production and verifiable justification.<1>p. 736</1>
The fourth mechanism is technical expert examination oriented to functional impact, and not to the total engineering of the ecosystem.<1>p. 661</1>

I complain, and the answer never solves anything. What can I do? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I complain, and the answer never solves anything.</1> <2>What can I do?</2>

Customer service is kind, answers quickly and asks you to wait, but the problem continues, and you end up letting it go. Often the conflict is managed before it becomes a complaint, and the friendly tone does not change what you lost.
In platform-governed ecosystems, the conflict does not begin when the user decides to litigate, complain or formalize dissatisfaction. In many cases, it is governed before that.<1>p. 780</1>

The user is not merely facing an opaque environment or criteria he does not control. He is facing an ecosystem that produces enough signals of intelligibility and care to induce accommodation, even when the materiality of enjoyment has already been compromised.<1>p. 782</1>
How do you know whether customer service is solving the problem or just calming you down?
Some signs come up again and again. The reply seems to explain but does not say what happened, and the tone is friendly, yet no way to contest the decision ever opens.

The loss is also often presented as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, a security measure or a normal stage of use. In a service you use every day, the small frustrations get absorbed one by one, until the loss seems normal.
The test is not whether you felt well treated. It is whether customer service works in a way that steers attention away from the loss and drains the force from your complaint.

The platform may, for example, offer a sense of transparency without delivering real intelligibility, produce an impression of listening without opening effective paths of contestation, mobilize a human tone without assuming proportional duties of reasoning or justification and distribute signs of care that work less as adequate information and more as semiotic cushioning of criticism.<1>p. 782</1>

The loss no longer appears as an exceptional event and comes to be metabolized as part of the normal functioning of the system. The same happens with friction. Instead of promptly triggering a reading of inadequacy or abusiveness, it may be reconfigured by the platform as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, an understandable inconvenience, a security measure, a necessary update or a simple stage of use.<1>p. 781</1>
Which conversations with customer service are worth keeping?

It is worth keeping the conversations with customer service, the canned replies and the justifications the company gave. It also helps to note the steps you were led through, such as waiting, trying again or accepting a vague explanation, because they show how the loss was handled.

The evidence compatible with this subtype requires reconstruction of the discursive and procedural environment in which frustration becomes legible or, on the contrary, is diluted. This includes the analysis of the language of the interface, of the customer service flows, of the response templates, of the routines of explanation, of the way the platform frames the loss and of the steps through which the user is led to accept, wait, relativize or close the dissatisfaction.<1>p. 782-783</1>
What can you ask for to get the complaint moving?

You may ask the company to explain clearly what happened and why, giving the concrete reason for the decision. You may also ask it to offer a way to contest that genuinely deals with your complaint instead of just soothing you.

The original complaint still stands. If the problem was the account, the item or the charge, your request about it still holds, because customer service that merely soothes you does not erase the conflict.

The legal response compatible with this picture tends to require more than simple retrospective repair. It may call for correction of customer service flows, reinforced intelligibility, prohibition of functionally misleading discursive routines, procedural duties of reasoning and the design of paths of contestation that do not serve only to absorb dissatisfaction, but to make it effectively processable and verifiable.<1>p. 783</1>

The conflict does not disappear. It is governed in its pre-legal phase, through mechanisms that turn loss into tolerable noise, opacity into normality and asymmetry into an absorbable experience.<1>p. 782</1>
Where should you take the complaint when customer service just goes in circles?

When the conversation with the company just goes in circles, it may be better to take the complaint elsewhere, to Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, routes explained on the channels page. Waiting for customer service itself to acknowledge the loss may leave the problem unanswered, since the company also influences when the loss becomes visible.

There, the saved conversations show how customer service handled the case. And when the same way of answering affects many people, public consumer protection agencies can demand complaint procedures that everyone can understand.
Contestation may be postponed, demobilized or dissolved before it takes institutional form.<1>p. 782</1>
Is kind customer service a problem?

No. Simple language, polite service and the company's effort to keep a good relationship with you are not illegal. The problem begins when this style of service becomes a structural part of a way of draining conflicts of their force.
Nor is there any guarantee that the complaint will succeed. What changes is that the loss is no longer treated as noise and becomes, once again, a problem that can be examined.

The problem does not lie in the use of accessible language, in polite service or in the legitimate attempt to maintain a functionally stable relationship with the user. The problem begins when these elements come to form, structurally, part of a regime of practical neutralization of conflict.<1>p. 782</1>

My reach dropped or I was punished on a social network. Is there anything I can ask for? · Lex Plataformae
<1>My reach dropped or I was punished on a social network.</1> <2>Is there anything I can ask for?</2>

On a social network, what you see and how many people see what you post, known as reach, depend on the platform's own rules. When reach drops, a post disappears or the account is punished, the issue may go beyond the post itself and extend to the way the platform governs what appears.

Meta's Terms of Service describe an environment in which the use of Facebook is subject to private rules of permanence, visibility, sharing, moderation and organization of circulating content, so that the user's experience is mediated by internal criteria of distribution and management of social interaction <1>FACEBOOK</1><2>(Facebook, [202-?])</2>.<3>p. 762</3>
How do you know whether the drop in reach or the punishment went too far?

Every network adjusts what appears, and change is not a problem in itself. There may be a problem when the change alters the visibility logic, the reputation criteria or the circulation rules. It matters when it significantly downgrades what the network offered as a place of reach and recognition, with nothing to make up for the loss.

Punishment works in a similar way. Your access, your permanence, your visibility and your chance to complain may depend on punishments no one explains. When that happens, or when the way back is much harder than the way in, it is a sign that the power to punish may be misused.

Functional equivalence, in turn, applies when changes to the intermediation regime, the visibility logic, the reputational criteria or the circulation rules significantly degrade the utility legitimately incorporated into the relationship, without compatible restoration. This can occur both in e-commerce and in the social circulation of content, whenever the platform substantially changes the functional role of the infrastructure it offered as an environment of exchange, reach or recognition.<1>p. 764</1>
Which records help show the drop or the punishment?

Dated screenshots help, showing the reach numbers before and after, the punishment notice, the rule the network cited and your messages with customer service. It is also worth keeping the affected content, the way to contest that existed and what the measure did to your use of the network.

What weighs most, however, is the way the feed, the recommendations and the reputation system shape what circulates, and that data stays with the network. That is why it is not reasonable to expect you to give detailed proof of something that was never within your reach.

In social networks, this reconstruction may also involve examining the way the feed, recommendation, reach and reputational management condition the very perception of what is in circulation.<1>p. 763</1>
What can you ask the network for after the punishment or the drop?

If the punishment has no reason that can be checked and no reasonable way to contest it, you may be entitled to have it reviewed or reversed. You can also ask the network to create or improve a real way for you to defend yourself.

You can also ask for minimum clarity about the moderation criteria, meaning the review of what may stay online, and about the criteria for distributing what appears. This does not oblige the network to open its internal systems, but it must be enough for you to understand how the decision affected you and to contest it.

Open auditability requires minimum institutional verifiability of the relevant criteria of presentation, prioritization, moderation, reputation and circulation, without this implying unrestricted opening of internal systems. What is demanded is sufficient intelligibility to understand how the environment organizes the user's experience and how certain choices of the platform interfere in the formation of expectation, in the comparability between alternatives and in the possibility of contestation.<1>p. 764</1>
Who can you turn to when the network does not explain the punishment?

The first route is usually the network's own channel for contesting decisions, in writing and with the screens saved. A kind reply that mentions a technical adjustment or a security measure is not an explanation. And feeling heard is not the same as having a real way to contest.

When the same punishment policy hits many accounts without explanation, the response can be collective and reach the whole punishment system. Procon, Consumidor.gov.br, the Public Prosecutor's Office and the Public Defender's Office appear on the channels page.
When can the network punish you or change your reach without that giving you a claim?

The network has the power to punish and to organize what appears, but that power alone is not enough. It needs a reason that can be checked, consistency from one decision to the next and an understandable way to contest it.

A small or passing drop is not enough, because the loss needs to be significant and lasting, not a one-day nuisance. Nor does every relationship conducted through technology fall under consumer protection.
There is a typical possibility of significant degradation of the bundle without a total loss of access, in a persistent and substantive way, rather than as a one-off discomfort.<1>p. 433</1>

The rule that harmed me was buried in the terms of use. Now what? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The rule that harmed me was buried in the terms of use.</1> <2>Now what?</2>

The company says the rule was in the terms of use, which are the contract you accept when you create the account or make a purchase. Having it written somewhere is not enough, because what counts is whether, when you made your decision, you could understand what that rule meant.
The mere accumulation of texts, links, notices, policies, terms and explanatory windows does not, by itself, satisfy the requirement of adequate information.<1>p. 722</1>
How do you know whether the rule was really hidden?
Information can fail in three ways. There can be so much text that the essentials get lost among everything else, or the rule can be scattered across documents, screens and menus that do not connect.

The third way is the screen flow itself, which highlights what attracts you and pushes what works against you to places almost no one looks. In all three cases the rule exists, but it does not inform.
The question, then, is whether the rule appeared clearly and at the moment when it could change your decision to buy, to continue or to react.

Informational inadequacy may thus take the form of excess, dispersion and flow architecture. Excess, when textual overload makes it impractical to distinguish the essential from the accessory. Dispersion, when the relevant elements of the relationship are fragmented across multiple documents, screens and paths without sufficient integration.<1>p. 722</1>

The legally relevant question is no longer whether a given piece of information was somewhere in the supplier's documentary ecosystem. It becomes whether that information was made accessible, comprehensible and relevant at the moment it could influence the legitimate formation of the consumer's expectation or reaction.<1>p. 723</1>
Which screens show how the rule reached you?

It helps to keep a record of the path you took before accepting or buying, with the screens, buttons and notices and where the link to the terms was. It is also worth saving the version of the terms in force that day, because these texts change over time.

If the rule came in a patch note, which is the text the company publishes when it changes the service, it is worth saving that note and the date it was published. Publishing the note is not enough when the change affects the core of what you use.

The consumer does not find just a single, centralized and stable contractual text. The consumer faces successive interface flows, scattered notices, secondary menus, help centers, versioned policies, partial explanations, promotional communications, contextual notifications and later changes that redesign the informational field without offering a material synthesis of what changed.<1>p. 722</1>
What can you ask for when the rule was not properly disclosed?

You may ask the company to correct the way it informs, put what matters in plain view and show what it actually displayed to you. You may also ask for what you lost because of the lack of clarity to be restored.

Depending on the case, the obscure rule may cease to apply against you. Consumer law says that a contract does not bind you when you had no real chance to learn its content beforehand, or when it was written in a way that makes it hard to understand.
When the text is confusing, the confusion may weigh against the company, because it drafted the contract and you had no way to negotiate.

The CDC already contains the normative core of this problem. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information. This means that the technical complexity of the supply does not authorize the supplier to hide behind indecipherable vocabulary, documentary cascades or communicational architectures that deliver words and withhold meaning. Likewise, consumer contracts do not bind the consumer when the consumer is not given a real opportunity to learn of their content beforehand, nor when they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope.<1>p. 601</1>
What is asked for is correction of the decision environment, neutralization of obscurity, production of records and restoration of the affected enjoyment.<1>p. 609</1>

Pre-drafted clauses must be read so as to respect the legitimate interests of those who accepted them without being able to negotiate them, and obscure drafting triggers precisely the presumption that the supplier failed in its duty to organize consent on a fair basis.<1>p. 604</1>
Where can you show that the rule was hidden?
The complaint to the company can ask it to show where and when the rule was presented to you. If the answer is only that everything was in the contract, it confuses existing with informing.

Outside the company, the case can be taken to Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, routes detailed on the channels page. When the same rule affects all customers, the correction can reach everyone through action by public consumer protection bodies.

The centrality of verifiable adequacy also prevents the supplier's standard defense from resting on the claim that “everything was in the contract”. This formula confuses formal existence with material fulfillment of the duty.<1>p. 723</1>
Is every long contract illegal?
No. The question is whether an ordinary person could read and understand what the rule meant, what rights and duties it created and what consequences it carried.
Nor is the question whether or not you read it. It is whether, given how the information was organized, it could guide your decision.
Having the rule in the contract does not save the company, but it does not condemn it on its own either, because everything depends on how the whole was organized.

What matters is whether the average consumer could read and understand what those clauses meant, which rights and obligations were being assumed and which practical consequences followed from adherence.<1>p. 604</1>

In environments of high informational complexity, the contract may even contain a nominal reference to the disputed risk, change or limitation, and still fail to inform adequately if the organization of the communicational whole produces noise, minimizes the impact of the relevant information or makes its practical connection with the consumer's decision unworkable.<1>p. 723</1>
