I want to leave, but I would lose everything I built there. Does that count? · Lex Plataformae
<1>I want to leave, but I would lose everything I built there.</1> <2>Does that count?</2>

You think about quitting the game, the network or the service, but leaving means losing your rank, your reputation, your history and the ties that only exist in there. That cost of leaving counts, and it helps explain why the company has greater duties toward those who already depend on the environment.
How do you know whether the cost of leaving has started to trap you?

Leaving an ordinary service just means switching suppliers. Here it is different, because the history, the rank, the signs of prestige and the ties you made stay with the company and only matter in there. Leaving interrupts your recognizable existence in that world.

This cost goes beyond money and convenience, because it includes losing the continuity of your story and the positions of recognition you hold there. None of this assumes that you are truly trapped or unable to act, since what counts is dependence in practice. And finding it hard to quit is not a weakness on your part, but a predictable effect of an environment that measures, compares and rewards those who stay.

The clearest sign appears when the company changes the rules and you accept only because leaving would cost more. In a long relationship like this, your yes after the change is often no more than forced acceptance of the new state of affairs.

The exit barrier can be described as a form of social death within the ecosystem. The expression does not operate as moral dramatization, but as a functional description of the effect produced when the platform concentrates the records that sustain belonging and relevance, that is, history, repertoire, ranked position, signs of prestige, community ties and traces of participation. Leaving the environment, under these conditions, is not like migrating from one service to another, because it implies interrupting one's own socially recognizable existence in that world, with loss of symbolic continuity and practical erasure of marks of trajectory that have become a condition of public commensurability.<1>p. 359</1>

In this same register, symbolic identity and personal integrity are connected by two effects of dependence that can be named symbolic captivity and identity captivity. [...] The second designates the form of dependence in which the cost of exit is not limited to financial or convenience dimensions, because it implies loss of narrative continuity and of positions of recognition whose existence takes place, decisively, within the ecosystem, through networks, histories, roles and internal circuits of value.<1>p. 466</1>
What is worth recording before deciding to leave?

It is worth recording your history, your rank, your badges and titles, your inventory and the rewards that only you have, with screenshots and dates. Once the account is gone or left behind, all that remains to show what existed is statements, emails, old screenshots and memory.

What shows the weight of what you built is not the sadness of leaving, but the value the system itself gives to it, through badges, visibility, requirements for taking part and reputation. Before leaving, you can also ask the company to confirm what data it keeps about you and give you access to it, as well as portability, which is the transfer of that data.
What can you ask for when both staying and leaving are costly?

When the company changes something important in what you use, it must give notice with ample, clear and timely information. The reason is that, for those who depend on the environment, leaving, adapting or contesting is never neutral.

This dependence reinforces the company's duties to be transparent, to let you contest, to make changes checkable and to restore what you lost. The weight of these duties is proportional to the power it exercises over the environment.

The design of the environment may exploit the cost of leaving, together with hard cancellation paths, manufactured urgency and lack of clarity. When this is repeated as a method, consumer law may treat the whole as an abusive practice. The request may then extend to correcting the design itself.

When the company modifies content, quality, parameters or relevant conditions of enjoyment, it must offer ample, intelligible and timely information, precisely because the consumer is placed in a relationship of practical dependence in which the cost of exit, adaptation or contestation is not neutral <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>.<3>p. 658</3>
Who can you turn to when leaving means losing everything?
The first place to go is the company itself, which must respond to your request for your data and to your challenge to changes that weighed on what you had.

If it does not respond, the case can be taken to Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court, routes detailed on the channels page. Since the cost of leaving is usually the same for all users, the response can also be collective, through a class action or through public consumer protection bodies.
How far does protection go for someone who wants to leave?

Not every intense relationship with a game is a problem, and keeping customers with challenges and rewards is not illegal in itself. What counts is when this raises the cost of leaving in a way that can be shown.

The rank exists while the account and the service exist, and data protection does not make you the owner of everything the company records. Small frustrations and normal changes to the service are also left out, because the loss needs to be significant, lasting and describable by checkable criteria.
It also presupposes secure management of relevant records and trails. These provisions do not turn the consumer into the absolute owner of everything the platform records<1>p. 542</1>

The service got worse, and the price is still the same. Can I complain? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The service got worse, and the price is still the same.</1> <2>Can I complain?</2>

You pay the same as before but get less, because the service lost features, tightened limits, got slower or started demanding more to deliver the same thing. The name and the price stayed the same while the delivery shrank, and consumer law treats as void any change the company makes on its own to the content or quality of what it sells.
How can you tell the decline is not just your impression?

A course that cuts half its classes in the middle of the semester and keeps charging the same price does what anyone would find wrong. On platforms the cut almost never goes by that name, and instead shows up as reduced reach, performance degraded little by little, features that disappear and tighter limits.

This applies to any service that lasts over time, such as subscriptions, apps and software. It applies even to devices that receive firmware updates, firmware being the internal program that makes the device work. What brings these cases together is not the sector, but the way each service organizes access and what you expect from it.
What counts is a persistent and significant decline that takes away the essentials of what you signed up for. The shell of the service can stay intact while its content has been hollowed out.

Commenting on art. 51, XIII, Nunes asks, in a deliberately blunt way, how it would be possible to change a contract unilaterally and still give the change legal validity <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</2>. The example he offers, of the supplier that cuts classes while keeping the same price <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</4>, works as an objective yardstick for platforms.<5>p. 479-480</5>

The example of updates that degrade accessibility and compatibility in software or firmware helps visualize the structure of the problem. In these cases, no one seriously argues that every update is unlawful. What is at issue is whether, under the pretext of improvement, the update significantly compromises the use, performance or compatibility of goods still within their expected durability, without adequate information, without effective consent and without means of mitigation.<1>p. 655</1>

What matters is not whether the platform presents itself as a cognitive tool, market infrastructure, productive environment or reputation system, but how it organizes access, modulates expectations, distributes risks and conditions the possibility of institutional reconstruction of the conflict.<1>p. 756</1>
In less pompous and more useful language: it is not enough to leave the shell of the relationship intact if the content enjoyed has been hollowed out.<1>p. 651</1>
How do you record a decline that creeps in gradually?

It is worth keeping the description of the plan or offer from the day you signed up, with what was included. Dated screenshots showing the before and after also help. The change notices the company sent count too, because it should have told you the essentials in time for you to understand and react.

Noting the day you noticed the decline also helps, since in a continuous service the loss may only show up with prolonged use. And you do not need to have everything filed, because the history of versions and decisions stays with the company.
The count must track the real moment at which the inadequacy becomes knowable, above all when it only emerges with prolonged use or with the supervening deterioration of serviceability<1>p. 558</1>
The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives only communicational fragments<1>p. 471</1>
What can you ask for when the delivery shrank but the charge did not?

The request can start with restoring the service to the level you signed up for. That can mean undoing the change, offering an alternative version or swapping it for something that serves the same function. It can also mean correcting the settings or keeping compatibility with what you already use.

Depending on the case, the decline may be a quality defect that reduces the value of the service. The law then also lets you ask for an abatement, which is a proportional discount on the price, or end the contract without a penalty. You do not need to argue over whether the company was at fault.

You can also ask the company to say what changed, when and why, instead of just answering that the service evolved. When it speaks of an update or an improvement, what needs to be shown is that the essentials were preserved.

Faced with quality defects that reduce the value of the service, the consumer may demand termination of the contract without penalty or a proportional abatement of the price, with no need to discuss the supplier's fault, since this is strict liability <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 354])</2>.<3>p. 563</3>
Where can you take a complaint about a service that got worse for everyone?

The complaint starts with the company itself, and continuing to pay does not mean you accepted the decline. When the change is significant, it should have been communicated in a way you could understand, and your silence does not count as agreement.

When the decline hits all customers at once, it is the kind of problem that can go to Procon, the Public Defender's Office or the Public Prosecutor's Office, presented on the channels page. In these cases the response can fix the service for everyone, rather than just repairing your case.
When does a change in the service give you no grounds to complain?

Services that last for years need to change, and switching the means or the method can be legitimate and even necessary for them to remain viable. The limit is using the change to shift onto you risks that belong to the company, to lower the quality or to cut relevant features.

A one-day fluctuation or a small adjustment is not enough, and not every reduction is illegal. Nor can one assume that every digital service causes this problem with the same force, because each case depends on how that service works.

Changes of means and method may be legitimate, and sometimes necessary, to keep the supply viable. The limit is that they cannot be used to shift structural risks onto the consumer, degrade quality, restrict relevant features, erode conditions of access or reconfigure regimes of participation and recognition that were part of economically stabilized enjoyment.<1>p. 480</1>
Was there a marginal loss, within the ordinary evolution of the service, or was there a substantial emptying of the functional core of enjoyment? Not every reduction is unlawful.<1>p. 653</1>

The point, here, is not to gather digital examples under a single heading out of mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment.<1>p. 755</1>

The company says I only have a license. So I didn't buy anything? · Lex Plataformae
<1>The company says I only have a license.</1> <2>So I didn't buy anything?</2>

You paid, the button said buy, and the contract calls what you received a license, meaning a permission to use that can be withdrawn. The label in the contract does not by itself decide your protection, because consumer law also treats things with no physical form as products.
How can you tell whether the word license is being used against you?

It happens when you complain that something disappeared or got worse and the answer is that you never had anything, because it was all a permission that could evaporate. Things with no physical form are also goods in the eyes of the law, and when real money changed hands the word license is not enough to erase what you received.

The contract itself usually helps you. The same terms of use that speak of a license acknowledge that there is content linked to your account, such as currency, skins and other items. And they admit that you may have bought it, earned it or received it as a gift.

What decides your protection is neither the fact that the item is digital nor the name the company gives it. It is how much what you use depends on an environment that the platform maintains, adjusts and can change. That dependence bears on your access, on your ability to stay and on what you are able to understand.

When there is actual economic outlay or relevant incorporation of utility into the subject's sphere, the language of the license is not enough to erase the legal density of the asset, nor to neutralize the application of public policy rules <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 124; p. 193)</2>.<3>p. 573</3>
Which documents show what you actually received?

It is worth keeping the proof of payment and the purchase screen showing the word the button used. A screenshot of the inventory or library with what is in your account also helps. This shows that you made your decision based on the language of a purchase, even if the contract speaks of a license.
Keep the terms of use from the day of purchase as well, because that is where the company acknowledges the content linked to your account and the ways of obtaining it.
What can you ask for when the answer is that it was all just a license?

Your request can start by asking for the case to be handled under consumer law, with what you bought treated as an immaterial product, that is, a product with no physical form. The service the company provides does not erase this, because it is precisely how the company maintains and updates what it sold.

Once the case is treated as the purchase of a product, you can demand that what was promised keep being delivered over time. Even the account termination clause of a major game states that losing access does not affect any rights you may have under consumer protection laws.

The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, without the service dimension of the relationship ruling out control of enjoyment as the core of the supply.<3>p. 743</3>
Who decides whether the license sets aside your rights?

Not the company alone. The case stays within consumer law, with no need for a new law for the digital world. That is why it follows the same paths as any consumer complaint, starting with the company and moving on, if needed, to Procon, Consumidor.gov.br or the Small Claims Court.

If your question is about inheritance, about what happens to an account after someone dies or about passing the item on, that is a different conversation. These disputes are usually handled under the rules of civil law, which deal with who owns what.
